mcqs.question: A schema migration adds a column that a downstream service needs to read. In what order should the migration and the service deploy?
options: The migration must land first, so the column exists before any deployed code tries to read it
The service deploy must land first, since code changes are always safer to ship first
Order doesn't matter as long as both happen within the same day
The migration and the deploy must happen in the exact same second to avoid any gap
mcqs.explanation: Reading a column that doesn't exist yet fails immediately, so the migration has to land first. Deploying the reading code first would be the unsafe order; simultaneous timing isn't achievable or necessary once the correct sequence is respected.

mcqs.question: Why is 'trigger every service's pipeline at the same time' considered an anti-pattern for a multi-service release?
options: It's actually the fastest and safest way to release when you have many services
It removes any explicit ordering or staging, so a dependency mistake or a slow deploy can cascade into a hard-to-diagnose outage spanning multiple services and owners
It only fails if the services are owned by different teams
The problem is purely about CI resource contention, not correctness
mcqs.explanation: The risk is correctness, not speed or resource contention: without explicit dependency ordering or staged rollout, a multi-service release has no safeguard against services landing in an order that breaks a contract between them -- and the resulting failure is harder to trace than a single-service bug.

mcqs.question: Service B has already deployed against a new contract from service A. Why might rolling A back to its previous version now be unsafe?
options: Rollback is unsafe for any service once any other service has deployed anything
It's only unsafe if A and B are owned by different teams

If A's previous version doesn't satisfy N+1/N-1 compatibility with what B now expects, B can start failing against the rolled-back A -- the rollback needs to preserve compatibility in both directions, not just revert one side
Rollback is always safe as long as it happens within the same release train
mcqs.explanation: The N+1/N-1 rule exists precisely so a rollback stays safe even after a dependent service has moved forward -- the risk is compatibility direction, not team ownership or release-train timing, which don't determine whether the previous version of A can still serve B's current requests.

mcqs.question: A codebase has accumulated a dozen backwards-compatibility shims from past multi-service migrations, each originally meant to live for one release cycle. What's the root cause?
options: The compatibility-shim pattern itself is flawed and should be avoided in future migrations
N+1/N-1 compatibility rules force shims to be permanent by design

Removing the shim (step 3 of a safe rollout) has no deadline or user-facing symptom if skipped, so without a tracked owner and date it silently never gets prioritized against work that does have a deadline
This only happens in organizations without a release train
mcqs.explanation: The shim pattern is correct and necessary during a rollout -- the failure is organizational: cleanup has no forcing function, so it loses to deadlined work indefinitely. A release train doesn't fix this on its own; only treating removal as a tracked, owned step does.
